location.value: Central Europe: Austria, Bohemia, Hungary, Croatia, and at times the Low Countries and parts of Italy, ruled from Vienna. Under Charles V it also held Spain and its empire.

terrain.value: The Danube basin (it was called the “Danube Monarchy”), the Alps, the Bohemian plateau and the Hungarian plain.

resources.value: Bohemian and Hungarian farmland, silver and mineral mines, and later Bohemian industry.
resources.source: Evans, Austria, Hungary, and the Habsburgs (2006)

disasters.value: Plague outbreaks (e.g. Vienna 1679) and wars with the Ottomans.
disasters.source: Evans, Austria, Hungary, and the Habsburgs (2006)

population.value: Not given in the Wikipedia infobox. The monarchy’s lands held roughly 20–25 million people by the late 18th century.
population.source: Evans, Austria, Hungary, and the Habsburgs (2006)

urbanisation.value: Vienna was the dynastic capital (Prague in 1583–1611). Other cities included Prague, Budapest, Milan and Brussels.

disease.value: Plague waves, including the Great Plague of Vienna (1679).
disease.source: Evans, Austria, Hungary, and the Habsburgs (2006)

migration.value: Resettlement of lands retaken from the Ottomans (e.g. German settlers in Hungary and the Banat in the 18th century).
migration.source: Evans, Austria, Hungary, and the Habsburgs (2006)

economicBase.value: Agriculture on noble estates with serf labour, mining, and later textiles and industry in Bohemia and Austria.
economicBase.source: Evans, Austria, Hungary, and the Habsburgs (2006)

tradeRoutes.value: The Danube and Alpine routes, Adriatic ports (Trieste), and the Low Countries’ trade.
tradeRoutes.source: Evans, Austria, Hungary, and the Habsburgs (2006)

wealth.value: No GDP estimate is given in the sources checked.

moneyAndTax.value: The gulden/florin and the thaler (the Maria Theresa thaler became a widely used trade coin). Taxes depended on bargaining with the provincial estates until 18th-century reforms.
moneyAndTax.source: Evans, Austria, Hungary, and the Habsburgs (2006)

inequality.value: Great noble landowners over serfs. Joseph II abolished personal serfdom in 1781, and remaining feudal obligations ended in 1848.
inequality.source: Evans, Austria, Hungary, and the Habsburgs (2006)

governmentType.value: A composite monarchy, a “union of crowns” with only partly shared institutions, ruled by the House of Habsburg from Vienna.

keyRulers.value: Rudolf I (1282). Maximilian I. Charles V (1519–1556). Ferdinand I (1556–1564). Maria Theresa (1740–1780). Joseph II (1780–1790). Francis II/I (1792–1835). Franz Joseph I (from 1848).

succession.value: Hereditary in the Habsburg (from 1740, Habsburg-Lorraine) family, via strategic marriages. The Pragmatic Sanction allowed Maria Theresa to inherit.

institutions.value: Each land kept its own estates and laws. Centralising reforms came under Maria Theresa and Joseph II. Unified as the Austrian Empire in 1804, then reorganised by the 1867 Compromise.

stability.value: The Bohemian revolt, crushed at White Mountain (1620). Hungarian revolts. The revolutions of 1848–49, suppressed.

eliteConflict.value: Tension between the dynasty and the estates and nobles of Bohemia and Hungary over rights and religion.
eliteConflict.source: Evans, Austria, Hungary, and the Habsburgs (2006)

armyAndTech.value: A large multi-ethnic army and the Military Frontier against the Ottomans.
armyAndTech.source: Evans, Austria, Hungary, and the Habsburgs (2006)

majorWars.value: Wars with the Ottomans (sieges of Vienna 1529 and 1683, then the Treaty of Karlowitz 1699). The Thirty Years’ War. The War of the Spanish Succession. The War of the Austrian Succession. The Napoleonic Wars. Defeats in 1859 and 1866.

territoryChange.value: Gained Bohemia and Hungary (1526), retook Hungary from the Ottomans (1683–1699), lost Silesia to Prussia (1740–42), and lost Lombardy (1859) and Venetia (1866).

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals: the Ottoman Empire, France, Prussia and Sweden. Allies: Spain (the Habsburg branch), Russia and Britain at times.

inventions.value: Not a major centre of invention before the 19th century. It supported astronomy at Rudolf II’s court in Prague (Tycho Brahe, Kepler).
inventions.source: Evans, Austria, Hungary, and the Habsburgs (2006)

scienceEducation.value: Universities (Vienna 1365, Prague 1348). Maria Theresa introduced compulsory primary schooling (1774).
scienceEducation.source: Evans, Austria, Hungary, and the Habsburgs (2006)

openness.value: The Counter-Reformation favoured Catholicism, but Joseph II’s Patent of Toleration (1781) eased restrictions on Protestants and Orthodox Christians.
openness.source: Evans, Austria, Hungary, and the Habsburgs (2006)

religion.value: Roman Catholicism was official, and the Counter-Reformation was strongly promoted. Protestant, Orthodox and Jewish minorities.

languageWriting.value: German, Hungarian, Czech, Latin and many other languages across its lands.
languageWriting.source: Evans, Austria, Hungary, and the Habsburgs (2006)

artsArchitecture.value: Baroque palaces and abbeys (Schönbrunn, Melk), and the Viennese classical music of Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven.
artsArchitecture.source: Evans, Austria, Hungary, and the Habsburgs (2006)

socialStructure.value: Dynasty, high nobility, clergy, townspeople, and serfs on noble estates.
socialStructure.source: Evans, Austria, Hungary, and the Habsburgs (2006)

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to the dynasty and Catholic Church rather than one nation. Motto: A.E.I.O.U.

neighbours.value: The Holy Roman Empire (whose crown the Habsburgs held almost continuously from 1438 to 1806), France, the Ottoman Empire, Poland, Prussia, Venice and Spain.

ideasReligions.value: A centre of the Catholic Counter-Reformation and later of Enlightenment reforms (Joseph II).
ideasReligions.source: Evans, Austria, Hungary, and the Habsburgs (2006)

colonisation.value: Expanded mainly through marriage and inheritance (“Let others wage war; you, happy Austria, marry”). It had no large overseas empire after the Spanish branch separated.

riseSignals.value: Dynastic marriages (Burgundy, Spain, Bohemia, Hungary), election as Holy Roman Emperors, and defence of Europe against the Ottomans.

peakPeriod.value: Greatest territorial extent under Charles V (1519–1556). A later high point around 1700–1790 after reconquering Hungary.

declineSignals.value: The loss of Silesia to Prussia, defeats by Napoleon, nationalist movements (1848), and defeats in 1859 and 1866, which ended Austrian dominance in Germany.

outcome.value: Transformation. It became the Austrian Empire (1804) and then Austria-Hungary (1867), which dissolved in 1918.

sources.value: Dynastic and state archives and modern histories. Checked against Wikipedia on 5 Nov 2026. See also Evans (2006). Wikipedia dates the monarchy 1282–1918; this entry covers 1526–1867, since Austria-Hungary has its own entry.

overallCertainty.value: Good for rulers and wars. Population and economic figures for the composite monarchy are rough. Some dates vary (e.g. the Low Countries acquired in 1477 or 1482).
